desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

Repeat the following until it is no longer possible: find the leftmost place where the values of pattern appear as consecutive nodes of the list, and delete those nodes (the nodes on both sides are then joined, which can create a new occurrence). Return the values of the remaining list.

For nums = [1,2,1,2,3,3,4] and pattern = [1,2,3] the leftmost occurrence is at positions 3 to 5 (1-indexed), and removing it leaves [1,2,3,4]. That list again contains the pattern, so one more removal leaves [4], which is the answer. An empty result is possible.
hints: Searching for the pattern again from scratch after every deletion works but can be O(n<sup>2</sup> * m). Deleting can only create a new match that ends right at the cut.
Process the nodes from left to right and keep the kept nodes on a stack. A match can only end at the node you just pushed, so you only need to know whether the top of the stack ends with the pattern.

Track, for every stack entry, how many pattern values match at the end of the stack up to that entry (the KMP state). When the state reaches len(pattern), pop that many entries; the state of the new top tells you where to continue.
editorial: Pushing nodes on a stack and removing a match the moment it is completed is equivalent to always removing the leftmost match: the match that ends first is also the one that starts first, because all matches have the same length. After a pop the stack is exactly what remains of the list to the left of the cut, so any new match must end at a later node.

To detect the end of a match in O(1) amortised time without rescanning, compute the KMP failure function of the pattern. Store with each stack entry the length k of the longest pattern prefix that is a suffix of the stack up to that entry. For a new value, start from the state of the top entry (0 for an empty stack), follow failure links while the next pattern value differs, and advance when it matches. If k reaches m, pop m entries; the stored state of the entry that is then on top is the state to continue from.

Building the failure function costs O(m) and the scan is O(n) amortised in the usual case. Because a pop restarts from a stored state, a single push can occasionally cost O(m) failure-link steps, so the worst case is O(n * m), which is only about 1.5 million steps under these constraints. Extra space is O(n + m).
